final_message:
I've written the report. About 88% of your farm's modelled emissions (roughly 3,710 of 4,217 t CO2e a year) come from the drained peat under your potatoes and wheat. Raising the water table on the potato ground is by far the biggest of your three options. Many of your details weren't in the question, so I filled them with assumptions you should check (listed below).

**Where the emissions come from (t CO2e a year)**

| Source | Farm total |
|---|---|
| Potatoes on drained peat (60 ha, about 37 t per hectare) | about 2,219 |
| Wheat on drained peat (40 ha, about 37 t per hectare) | about 1,493 |
| Cattle methane | about 439 |
| Sheep methane | about 65 |
| **Total the tools could model** | **about 4,217** |

Most of the peat emissions are CO2 from the peat breaking down because it is drained, plus some nitrous oxide. Nearly all the livestock methane comes from digestion rather than manure.

**What each option would cut (t CO2e a year)**

| Option | Saving |
|---|---|
| Keep growing potatoes, raise the yearly average water table from about 0.66 m to 0.45 m below the surface | about 770 |
| Keep growing potatoes, raise it to 0.30 m | about 1,410 |
| Rewet the potato ground to grow reed, water at about 0.20 m | about 2,100 |
| Feed additive for the cattle (sheep not included) | about 59 to 118 |
| 100 hedgerow trees, averaged over 50 years | about 0.4 to 1.0 |

- **Water table:** rewetting to reed would cut emissions from that ground by about 95% per hectare, but it ends potato growing there. The model doesn't say whether potatoes would grow well with water at 0.30 to 0.45 m. The reed figure assumes potato-level fertiliser, so the real saving is probably a bit larger.
- **Feed additive:** this is at most about 3% of the farm total. The 15% and 30% cuts in cattle methane are my assumptions for a mainly grazing suckler herd, not something the model worked out.
- **Hedgerow trees:** they take up 18 to 48 t CO2 in total over 50 years. That's small for climate, but the model doesn't count shelter, shade or wildlife benefits.

**Assumptions to check:**
- **Your fields:** your peat is drained to a typical Fenland level, with 200 kg of nitrogen fertiliser per hectare.
- **Your herd:** I assumed 85 calves, 20 breeding heifers, 40 steers, 20 heifers for slaughter, 2 bulls, 5 rams and 300 lambs.
- **Your hedges:** I assumed 3 km, with one new tree every 30 m (100 trees).
- **Your grass:** I treated the 80 ha of grass as not on peat. If it is drained peat, its emissions could be large.

The real total will be higher than 4,217 t CO2e. It leaves out the grass soil, nitrous oxide from manure and grazing, fuel, and bought-in fertiliser and feed.

**As a tenant:** raising water tables or changing what you grow on the peat will almost certainly need your landlord's consent. Carbon and nature credits, such as under the Peatland Code, usually belong to the landowner unless your tenancy says otherwise. The report covers schemes to look into, the tenancy points and where to get advice.

The report has two charts, one of the emission sources and one of the savings. It is at `/home/user/slate/demo/runs/farmer/20261118-2039-your-ely-farm-where-the-emissions-come-from-and-what-three-o.html`.
